_about: Facts for the knowledge quiz, checked by hand against the English Wikipedia article linked for each bird (text CC BY-SA 4.0). Edit tools/facts.json, not this file.

australian-magpie.diet: Insects, worms and other small creatures from the ground, plus some seeds and scraps
australian-magpie.fact: can recognise at least 100 different people, and rarely swoops the ones it knows

laughing-kookaburra.diet: Lizards, insects, worms, snakes and mice; it even takes goldfish from garden ponds
laughing-kookaburra.fact: has a laugh so famous it is used as a stock jungle sound effect in films

sulphur-crested-cockatoo.diet: Seeds, grain, fruit and shoots; it also chews soft timber and eats clay
sulphur-crested-cockatoo.fact: has learned to open wheelie bins in Sydney, a trick that spreads by imitation

galah.diet: Seeds gathered on the ground, mostly in the morning and late afternoon
galah.fact: gave Australian English its slang word for a fool

little-corella.diet: Seeds of grasses and crops such as wheat and barley, plus lawn grass
little-corella.fact: gathers in flocks whose screeching can be heard several kilometres away

yellow-tailed-black-cockatoo.diet: Seeds of she-oaks, banksias and pine cones, plus wood-boring grubs
yellow-tailed-black-cockatoo.fact: needs nest hollows in trees around 200 years old, so old trees matter to it

rainbow-lorikeet.diet: Nectar and pollen from eucalypt and other flowers, plus fruit
rainbow-lorikeet.fact: is the most commonly counted bird in BirdLife Australia’s annual Backyard Bird Count

crimson-rosella.diet: Seeds, fruit, nectar, berries and nuts, plus insects such as termites
crimson-rosella.fact: has green youngsters, and females sometimes destroy other pairs’ eggs to win a nest hollow

eastern-rosella.diet: Grass seeds, buds, flowers, nectar, fruit and insects
eastern-rosella.fact: escaped from cages in New Zealand around 1910 and is now established there

australian-king-parrot.diet: Fruit and seeds taken from trees or picked up off the ground
australian-king-parrot.fact: sits near the bottom of the pecking order when birds crowd a feeder

noisy-miner.diet: Nectar, fruit and insects, including manna, honeydew and lerp from gum leaves
noisy-miner.fact: drives smaller birds out of gardens so aggressively it has been called a ‘reverse keystone’ species

red-wattlebird.diet: Mainly nectar, topped up with insects, berries and fruit
red-wattlebird.fact: mops up nectar with a brush-tipped tongue of more than a hundred bristles

little-wattlebird.fact: is the smallest wattlebird and has no wattles at all

new-holland-honeyeater.diet: Nectar and honeydew, with spiders and insects for protein
new-holland-honeyeater.fact: was among the first Australian birds to be scientifically described, back in 1790

eastern-spinebill.diet: Nectar from gums, banksias and garden flowers, plus small insects
eastern-spinebill.fact: stores fat when flowers are plentiful to get through lean times

pied-currawong.diet: Berries, seeds, insects, eggs and small animals; it raids other birds’ nests
pied-currawong.fact: is named for its call, written down as ‘curra-wong’ or ‘kadow-kadang’

australian-raven.diet: Insects, carrion, small animals and whatever people leave behind
australian-raven.fact: built Australia’s highest recorded crow-family nest, on top of the AWA Tower in Sydney

magpie-lark.diet: Small creatures such as insects, worms and snails from lawns and mud
magpie-lark.fact: sings in duet, each partner adding a note half a second after the other

grey-butcherbird.diet: Insects, small lizards and birds, and occasionally fruit
grey-butcherbird.fact: wedges spare food into the fork of a branch to eat later

willie-wagtail.diet: Insects and other small arthropods, occasionally a small lizard
willie-wagtail.fact: fearlessly harasses birds far bigger than itself, kookaburras and eagles included

spotted-dove.diet: Grass seeds, grain, fallen fruit and the odd insect
spotted-dove.fact: was brought to Melbourne in the 1860s and has since spread along the east coast

crested-pigeon.diet: Seeds and grain, including those of the weed Paterson’s curse
crested-pigeon.fact: makes a whistling sound with its wings on take-off that warns other birds of danger

common-myna.diet: Insects, fruit, seeds and scraps from around people
common-myna.fact: was voted Australia’s ‘most important pest’ in a 2008 poll and nicknamed the ‘cane toad of the sky’

red-whiskered-bulbul.fact: was released in Sydney in 1880 and had spread through the suburbs by the 1920s

superb-fairywren.diet: Mostly insects, with some seeds, flowers and fruit
superb-fairywren.fact: was voted Australian Bird of the Year in 2021

welcome-swallow.fact: got its name from people welcoming its return as a sign of spring

silvereye.fact: crosses Bass Strait from Tasmania each winter to feed in Victoria and New South Wales

grey-fantail.diet: Flying insects caught in acrobatic chases
grey-fantail.fact: often builds several nests before laying, with seven in one season on record

spotted-pardalote.fact: nests underground, at the end of a tunnel dug into a bank

eastern-yellow-robin.diet: Insects and other small creatures pounced on from a low perch
eastern-yellow-robin.fact: is no relation to the European robin, despite the name

golden-whistler.fact: has been split into as many as 59 subspecies, one of the highest counts of any bird

eastern-whipbird.diet: Insects picked from the leaf litter
eastern-whipbird.fact: sings its whip-crack as a duet: the male cracks the whip and the female answers

eastern-koel.diet: Mostly fruit as an adult, especially figs
eastern-koel.fact: is a cuckoo whose chick, unlike most, does not push the host’s own chicks out of the nest

channel-billed-cuckoo.diet: Figs, mistletoe fruit and mulberries, plus insects and other birds’ eggs and nestlings
channel-billed-cuckoo.fact: is the world’s largest cuckoo and its largest brood parasite

black-faced-cuckooshrike.diet: Insects, caterpillars and other invertebrates, with some fruit and seeds
black-faced-cuckooshrike.fact: gathers in flocks of up to a hundred birds outside the breeding season

tawny-frogmouth.diet: Large night-flying insects, spiders, worms and small animals
tawny-frogmouth.fact: pairs for life and keeps the same territory for a decade or more

southern-boobook.diet: Mice, beetles, moths and small birds, caught by pouncing from a perch
southern-boobook.fact: is the smallest owl on the Australian mainland

australian-white-ibis.diet: Crayfish, mussels, insects and, in cities, scraps from bins
australian-white-ibis.fact: earned the nickname ‘bin chicken’, yet had no breeding records in Sydney until the 1980s

masked-lapwing.diet: Insects and worms found on the ground
masked-lapwing.fact: swoops people and animals that come near its nest in the breeding season

australian-brushturkey.diet: Scraps and compost in the suburbs, and whatever it rakes up from the leaf litter
australian-brushturkey.fact: checks the temperature of its compost-heap nest mound by sticking its beak in

superb-lyrebird.diet: Earthworms, insects and other invertebrates scratched from the forest floor, plus fungi
superb-lyrebird.fact: can mimic chainsaws, car alarms and camera shutters as well as other birds

satin-bowerbird.diet: Fruit above all, with leaves, seeds and insects
satin-bowerbird.fact: holds the longevity record for a banded songbird in the wild: twenty-six years

silver-gull.diet: Worms, fish, insects and crustaceans, and chips wherever people eat them
silver-gull.fact: thrives around shopping centres and rubbish tips as well as beaches

pacific-black-duck.diet: Seeds of water plants, plus small crustaceans, snails and insects
pacific-black-duck.fact: interbreeds with introduced mallards, which threatens it as a distinct species

australian-wood-duck.diet: Grasses, clover, herbs and grain, with the odd insect
australian-wood-duck.fact: is the only living member of its genus and looks more like a small goose than a duck

dusky-moorhen.diet: Seeds, water plants, algae, fruit, snails and other invertebrates
dusky-moorhen.fact: has a territorial call that carries more than two kilometres

australasian-swamphen.diet: Grasses and seeds, plus invertebrates and other birds’ eggs and chicks
australasian-swamphen.fact: practises joint laying, with several females adding eggs to one shared nest

australian-pelican.diet: Mainly fish, but also crustaceans, other birds and scraps
australian-pelican.fact: has the longest bill of any living bird, up to 50 cm

little-pied-cormorant.diet: Fish, crustaceans, eels and insect larvae
little-pied-cormorant.fact: sometimes drops a fish back on the water to turn it round and swallow it head first

white-bellied-sea-eagle.diet: Fish for about half its diet, plus carrion, seabirds and other animals
white-bellied-sea-eagle.fact: spans up to 2.2 metres across the wings and is one of Australia’s largest birds of prey
